q4.text: When did your periods last change or stop?

q7.text: Memory problems — forgetting names, words, or where you put things

q8.text: Word-finding difficulty — knowing what you want to say but not being able to find the word

q9.text: Reduced ability to multitask — struggling to manage more than one thing at a time

q10.text: Mood swings — feeling up and down for no clear reason

q11.text: Irritability — snapping or getting frustrated more easily than usual

q12.text: Feeling anxious or worried more than usual

q14.text: Low motivation — struggling to find the energy or desire to do things you used to enjoy

q15.text: Low self-worth — feeling less confident or less valuable than before

q16.text: Not feeling like yourself — not recognising the person you have become
q16.hint: This question catches many women for the first time. Trust what you feel.

q17.hint: You can answer honestly. If you're struggling, Mandi will put support on your roadmap right away.

q18.text: Hot flushes — sudden waves of heat through your body

q19.text: Night sweats — waking drenched or overheated

q20.text: Sleep problems — difficulty falling or staying asleep

q21.text: Heart palpitations — your heart racing or beating irregularly

q22.text: Headaches or migraines — more frequent or more severe than before

q24.text: Restless legs — an uncomfortable urge to move your legs, especially at night

q25.text: Tinnitus — ringing or buzzing in the ears

q26.text: Joint pain — aching, stiffness, or swelling in joints

q27.text: Muscle pain — generalised aching in muscles

q28.text: Frozen shoulder — pain or restricted movement in the shoulder
q28.hint: An under-recognised menopause symptom. If this is you, you are not imagining it.

q29.text: Fatigue and low energy — exhausted even after rest

q30.text: Weight gain — especially around the middle

q32.text: Skin changes — dryness, itchiness, or texture changes

q34.text: Dry eyes — persistent dryness, irritation, or blurry vision

q35.text: Changes in your period — heavier, lighter, longer, shorter, or more irregular than before

q38.text: Bladder issues — urgency, leaking, or needing to go more often, including at night

q41.text: Reduced alcohol tolerance — two glasses that used to be fine now feel like four
q41.hint: This is the question that makes women say: 'wait — that is menopause?'

q42.text: New or worsening allergies — hay fever, food intolerances, or sensitivities you never had before

q43.text: Worsening of a long-term health condition — asthma, migraine, autoimmune condition, or similar
q43.hint: If this is a strong yes, Mandi will route you to specialist-led care.

q44.text: Impact on your ability to work — concentration, productivity, or confidence at work

q45.text: Impact on your relationship with your partner

q46.text: Impact on your relationships with family — children, parents, close relatives

q47.text: Impact on your social life — withdrawing, not wanting to go out

q48.text: Impact on your ability to stay active and exercise

q49.text: When you think about what you have been experiencing — what is your gut feeling?
q49.a: Something is wrong and I need help now.
q49.b: It is probably just ageing — I will manage.
q49.c: I have tried everything. Nothing works for me.
q49.d: I have done my research — I know what is happening.

q50.a: Open to it if a doctor recommends it.
q50.b: I prefer natural approaches — herbs, lifestyle, supplements.
q50.c: I am nervous — I have heard it can be risky.
q50.d: I am already on HRT, or I have already tried it.

q51.b: My symptoms have been dismissed. I feel unseen.
q51.c: I prefer to research first before going to a doctor.
q51.d: I honestly do not know where to start.

q52.d: I had not thought about it.

facts.context: Perimenopause — the years of change before periods stop — most often lasts around 4 to 8 years, though for some women it is shorter or longer. Menopause itself is just one day.
facts.mind-cognition: Brain fog is one of the most common menopause symptoms — caused by shifting oestrogen, not by you losing your sharpness. For most women, it lifts.
facts.mood: Mood changes in menopause are physical, not a personal failing. Oestrogen interacts with serotonin, one of the brain's mood chemicals — so when hormone levels shift, mood can shift too.
facts.nervous-system: Hot flushes can begin years before your last period. Up to 8 in 10 women experience them — whatever you are feeling, you are far from alone.
facts.body: Joint and muscle aches are an under-recognised menopause symptom — oestrogen helps keep joints comfortable. Even frozen shoulder is linked to this change.
facts.urogenital: Unlike hot flushes, intimate and bladder symptoms tend not to fade on their own — but they respond very well to treatment. They are nothing to be ashamed of.
facts.other: Suddenly cannot tolerate alcohol the way you used to? Oestrogen interacts with histamine — the chemical behind allergy-type reactions — and some women notice new sensitivities in midlife. You are not imagining it.
facts.quality-of-life: Menopause symptoms ripple into work, sleep and relationships. Naming that impact is not complaining — it is the first step to getting the right support.
facts.mindset: It is never too late to ask for help. Some symptoms — including vaginal and bladder ones — respond well to treatment no matter how many years have passed since menopause.

about.title: A name that belongs to all of us.

name.heading: Mandi is the common thread that runs through us all.
name.p1: In Afrikaans, it is a short form of Amanda. In isiXhosa, it is drawn from Mandisa. Different languages, different communities, different lived experiences — and yet here we are, the same women, navigating the same bodies, deserving the same care.
name.p2: We chose a name beginning with M to anchor this project in Menopause — the life stage that sparked this mission. But Mandi was always meant to grow beyond that first chapter. Because hormonal health does not begin and end with menopause. It is a lifelong journey, and every woman deserves a trusted companion for the entirety of it.
name.p3: Mandi is that companion. For all of us.

story.heading: This platform was born from a personal story.
story.p1: In my late 40s, I mentioned heart palpitations to two older colleagues over lunch. One immediately suggested I see a heart specialist. The other said it was just part of getting older. Neither mentioned menopause. Neither mentioned that heart palpitations are one of the over 100 recognised symptoms of hormonal change. I had no idea.
story.p2: Soon thereafter I moved to Cape Town at the age of 50, ready for exciting new adventures. Instead, I ended up in hospital with a severe kidney infection caused by a bladder infection. I saw a urologist. My GP. A gynaecologist. Not one of them asked whether I was on HRT. Not one of them connected my recurring infections to my hormones — even though the link is well established. They treated my symptoms, not the cause.
story.p3: I endured years of joint pain, brain fog, mood swings, UTIs, painful sex, hot flushes, dry eyes, and many more symptoms.
story.p4: Then I went online. I found Dr Louise Newson. Dr Mary Claire Haver. Dr Lisa Mosconi. And many more. I started telling all my friends to find help. My husband calls me a menopause evangelist.
story.quote: Once you know better, you can do better.
story.p5: This motivated me to pitch a documentary series to kykNET called Meer As Warm Gloede — a four-part documentary series launching in August 2026. It breaks the silence around menopause in Afrikaans-speaking communities, tells real stories from real women, and gives viewers the knowledge and confidence to take their health into their own hands.
story.p6: The documentary opened doors. More research led me to discover MIDI in the United States — a platform that has recently achieved unicorn status, serving hundreds of thousands of women across all 50 states. That realisation set something in motion.
story.p7: I am now embarking on this journey with some incredible women to build our own South African equivalent: JoinMandi.com.

vision.heading: JoinMandi.com is more than a website. It is a movement.
vision.p1: It is the belief that every South African woman — in Parow or Polokwane, in Soweto or Stellenbosch, whether she speaks Afrikaans, isiZulu, isiXhosa, or any of the other languages that make this country extraordinary — deserves to understand what is happening in her own body, in a language that feels like home.
vision.p2: South Africa has 11 official languages. Most digital health platforms offer one: English. That is not good enough. Mandi is built to grow with the country — into every community where women have been left without informed answers and proper medical care.

hrt.title: The Truth About HRT
hrt.subhead: Fear travelled the world in 24 hours in 2002. The correction has taken 23 years. Here is what every woman deserves to know — in plain English.

compare.heading: Synthetic vs Body-identical
compare.intro: The most important thing women do not know is that not all HRT is the same. This distinction is the key to everything that follows.

synthetic.label: Synthetic / non-human HRT
synthetic.name: Premarin · Provera
synthetic.body: Premarin — made from horse urine — contains estrogens the human body does not naturally produce. Provera (MPA) — a synthetic progestin. Not the same molecule as human progesterone.
synthetic.note: This is what the 2002 WHI study tested.

bodyIdentical.label: Body-identical HRT
bodyIdentical.name: Estradiol · Micronised Progesterone
bodyIdentical.body: Estradiol (17β-estradiol) — derived from plants. Chemically identical to human oestrogen. Micronised progesterone (Prometrium / Utrogestan) — identical to human progesterone.
bodyIdentical.note: This is the recommended approach today.

timeline.heading: 1992 — Today
timeline.intro: A timeline of what actually happened — and what is changing now.

t1992.headline: Premarin peaks.
t1992.body: Premarin — made from the urine of pregnant mares — becomes the most prescribed drug in the US. The WHI study begins, testing Premarin plus Provera on 160,000 women.

t2002.headline: The study that changed everything — for the wrong reasons.
t2002.body: The WHI trial is stopped early. Global headlines declare HRT causes breast cancer. Use collapses by 80%. The absolute risk — 4 cases per 1,000 women over 5 years — is rarely mentioned. Results are applied to all HRT, including body-identical hormones that were never studied.

t2003.headline: Black-box warnings applied.
t2003.body: The FDA applies class-wide black-box warnings to all HRT products — including body-identical hormones that carry no such evidence of harm. A generation of women is denied treatment based on findings that do not apply to them.

t2008.headline: The pivotal French finding.
t2008.body: The E3N cohort study finds that body-identical progesterone does not increase breast cancer risk — unlike the synthetic progestin used in WHI. The problem in 2002 was never oestrogen — it was the specific synthetic used.

t2013.headline: Oestrogen alone reduces breast cancer risk.
t2013.body: A decade of WHI follow-up confirms estrogen-only HRT significantly reduces breast cancer incidence and mortality. This directly contradicts the 2002 message — but it takes ten years to reach the public.

t2015.headline: UK NICE recommends body-identical HRT.
t2015.body: Body-identical HRT — estradiol patches or gel with micronised progesterone — becomes the recommended approach. HRT prescriptions in England begin rising from this point.

t2025.headline: FDA removes the warnings.
t2025.body: The US HHS and FDA announce the removal of broad black-box warnings. The FDA states: women who start HRT within 10 years of menopause may reduce cardiovascular risk by up to 50%, Alzheimer's risk by 35%, and fracture risk by 50–60%.

mothers.title: Honour the Mothers
mothers.subhead: The moral centre of Mandi. A quiet, serious, deeply human acknowledgement that the platform women are using today stands on a foundation that has not always honoured women's bodies, voices, or choices.

baartman.body: A Khoikhoi woman taken from South Africa in 1810 and exhibited across Europe as a public spectacle. She died in Paris in 1815, aged 26. Her body remained on display in France until 1974. Nelson Mandela formally requested her return in 1994. On 9 August 2002 — National Women's Day — she was finally buried near her birthplace. She came home. She belongs to all of us.

anarcha.body: Three enslaved Black women whose names we know. Between 1845 and 1849 they were subjected to experimental surgery — Anarcha underwent at least 30 operations without anaesthesia — as the foundation of modern gynaecology was built on their suffering. In 2021, a 15-foot monument was erected in their honour. Their names are spoken now.

finding.heading: The women we are still finding.
finding.body: African women's bodies have been sites of medical research, colonial experimentation, and systemic neglect across centuries and across the continent. The specific stories are still being uncovered. As we find them, we will add them here. If you know a story that belongs on this page, we want to hear it.

wall.heading: Have you ever been dismissed? You are not alone.
wall.intro: Short stories submitted by Mandi users. Three sentences or less. Anonymous if they choose. Together they become something powerful.
wall.thandi: For three years I thought I was losing my mind. My doctor said I was stressed. Nobody said menopause.
wall.mariette: Ek het vyf jaar simptome gehad en nie geweet nie. Ek was nie besig om gek te word nie — my hormoon het verander.
wall.nomsa: My mother never spoke about this. Her mother never spoke about it. I want my daughter to have a different experience.

closing.names: Sarah Baartman. Anarcha. Betsey. Lucy. And every woman whose name was never written down.
closing.body: Their bodies carried the burden of a science that did not yet know how to treat them as human. Mandi is built in their honour. This page will keep growing — because there are more names to find, and more women to hear.

founder.quote: This platform was born from my own story — years of symptoms that nobody connected to my hormones. Once you know better, you can do better. And you can help others do the same.
